title: MTEL Physical Education (22) Practice Test - MTEL - Motor Learning and Skill Acquisition
subject: MTEL

questions.q: The ability to time movements to intercept a moving object, such as when catching a ball, is most dependent on an individual's ability to integrate motor behaviors with:
options: sensory information about the speed and direction of the object.
an understanding of how wind and air resistance affect the object's momentum.
visual information about the relative positions of body parts.
knowledge about the object's weight and the force with which it was propelled.
questions.explain: Intercepting a moving object requires integrating sensory input (like vision and hearing) about the object's speed and direction to properly time and direct body movements.
questions.subject: MTEL

questions.q: In a typical progression of motor skill development, which of the following skills is generally most difficult for children to master?
options: skipping
galloping
sliding
hopping
questions.explain: Skipping is a complex locomotor skill because it combines a step and a hop on the same foot in an uneven rhythm. It requires more coordination and balance than hopping, galloping, or sliding, and is typically mastered later.
questions.subject: MTEL

questions.q: Which of the following is characteristic of performance of an open motor skill?
options: The participant often performs the skill without having to respond to changing conditions.
The skill can only be performed as a continuous, repetitive skill rather than a discrete skill.
The participant often performs the skill in an unpredictable, changing environment.
The skill can be performed in precisely the same way each time regardless of the context.
questions.explain: An open motor skill is performed in a dynamic, unpredictable environment where conditions change, requiring the performer to adapt. Examples include playing soccer or basketball. In contrast, a closed motor skill is performed in a stable environment (e.g., diving).
questions.subject: MTEL

questions.q: A student is learning a new complex motor skill. The student will most likely benefit from the principle of transfer of learning if the:
options: new motor skill is similar to one already mastered.
student is open to feedback from both teachers and peers.
new motor skill is a discrete skill rather than a continuous one.
student has no preconceived notions about the motor skill.
questions.explain: The principle of **transfer of learning** states that prior knowledge of a skill will help in learning a new skill, especially if the skills share similar movement patterns or cognitive processes.
questions.subject: MTEL

questions.q: In which stage of motor learning are students typically capable of detecting errors in their own motor performance and taking steps to correct them, but cannot yet eliminate them?
options: cognitive stage
associative stage
autonomous stage
verbal stage
questions.explain: In the **associative stage**, the learner has grasped the fundamentals and works on refining the skill. They can often detect their own errors but haven't yet achieved automatic, error-free performance, which characterizes the autonomous stage.
questions.subject: MTEL

questions.q: Swimming strokes such as the crawl are defined as continuous or repetitive motor tasks because the:
options: skills are performed in a medium in which a greater degree of resistance is encountered than in air.
movement through the water can be sustained with no physical effort by keeping the body flat in the water.
strokes and kicking motions require unilateral rather than bilateral coordination.
recovery of the arms and legs leads directly into the next stroke, with no recognizable beginning and end.
questions.explain: A continuous or repetitive skill is cyclical, where the end of one cycle of movement flows directly into the beginning of the next. In the crawl stroke, the recovery phase of one arm movement initiates the next stroke.
questions.subject: MTEL

questions.q: Which of the following locomotor skills is typically most difficult for five year olds to perform?
options: jogging across the length of a classroom
walking along a low balance beam
hopping on one foot from one end of a classroom to the other end
walking along a circular pattern marked by tape on the floor
questions.explain: Hopping requires balancing on one foot, sustaining a period of non-support, and landing on the same foot. This requires more leg strength, coordination, and single-side balance than jogging or walking, making it more challenging for a five-year-old.
questions.subject: MTEL

questions.q: One important reason why a toddler learns to run several months after learning to walk is because in comparison to walking, running:
options: is a complex motor skill rather than a fundamental motor skill, and thus requires refinement.
is less stable and requires development of greater motor control and coordination.
requires one foot to be always in contact with the ground, which is difficult for toddlers to master.
involves supporting body weight in all phases, and thus requires additional strength.
questions.explain: Running includes a 'flight phase' where both feet are off the ground, making it inherently less stable than walking. It requires greater strength, balance, and motor control, which a toddler develops in the months after mastering walking.
